Question: How does the performance of the proposed model compare to other models when trained on the LDC2017T10 dataset, and what does this suggest about the effectiveness of incorporating syntax into the model?
Evidence:
[E1] (text, Section Table 1, page 4): Table 1: Parsing scores on LDC2017T10 dev set. Model Unlabelled F1 Labelled F1 Text-to-parse 87.5 85.8 AMR-to-parse 60.4 54.8 Unconditional 38.5 31.7
[E2] (text, Section 4, page 4): AMR-to-text model with the same architecture as above to control for the extra regularisation in our model compared to previous work. Our results show that adding syntax into the model dramatically boosts performance, resulting in state-ofthe-art single model performance on both datasets without using external training data. As an oracle experiment, we also generate from the realisation model conditioned on the ground truth parse. The outstanding result here – BLEU scores in the 50s – demonstrates that being able to predict the gold reference parse tree is a bottleneck in the performance of our model. However, given the inherent difﬁculty of predicting a single syntax realisation (cf. Section 4 ), we suspect that there is an intrinsic limit to how well generating from an AMR graph can replicate the reference realisation. We further note that we do not use models tailored to graph-structured data or characterlevel features as in Song et al. ( 2018 ); Beck et al. ( 2018 ), or additional unlabelled data to perform semi-supervised learning ( Konstas et al. , 2017 ). We believe that we can improve our results even further if we use these techniques.
[E3] (text, Section Table 3, page 4): Table 3: BLEU results for generation. Model Dev BLEU Test BLEU Trained on LDC2017T10 Our model 26.1 26.8 Our model + oracle parse 57.5 - Baseline s2s + copy 23.7 23.5 Beck et al. (2018) 22.8 23.3 Trained on LDC2015E86 or earlier + additional unlabelled data Song et al. (2018) - 33.0 Konstas et al. (2017) 33.1 33.8 Pourdamghani et al. (2016) 27.2 26.9 Song et al. (2017) 25.2 25.6

These claims failed the checks; write corrected claims to replace them:
- "The proposed model outperforms other models when trained on the LDC2017T10 dataset, as evidenced by its state-of-the-art single model performance on both datasets.": support check: The claim states that the model outperforms others on both datasets, but the evidence only mentions state-of-the-art performance on both datasets without external training data. The evidence does not specify that the model outperforms other models.
- "The performance of the proposed model is significantly enhanced by incorporating syntax, as shown by the dramatic boost in BLEU scores when using an oracle parse.": support check: The claim attributes the dramatic boost in BLEU scores to incorporating syntax, but the evidence attributes this to the ability to predict the gold reference parse tree, which is a bottleneck in the model's performance. The evidence does not directly support the claim that incorporating syntax enhances performance.
- "The proposed model's performance on the LDC2017T10 dataset is comparable to other models trained on earlier datasets, but it does not match the performance of models trained on more recent datasets or those using additional unlabelled data.": support check: The claim states that the model's performance is comparable to other models trained on earlier datasets and does not match more recent datasets or those using additional unlabelled data. The evidence shows that the model's BLEU scores are 26.1 and 26.8 for development and test sets, respectively, which are lower than the scores of other models trained on earlier datasets (e.g., 23.6 and 23.5 for the baseline model trained on LDC2015E86). However, the evidence does not provide a direct comparison to more recent datasets or those using additional unlabelled data, so the claim cannot be fully verified from the given evidence.
